title: Hidden content must not be keyboard focusable
summary: Something marked aria-hidden still contains a link or button that keyboard users can tab to. Hide it fully or make it unfocusable.
problem: An element has aria-hidden="true", which removes it from what screen readers announce, but it contains something focusable such as a link, button or input. The keyboard can still land on it even though assistive technology has been told it does not exist.
whoItAffects: Keyboard users tab onto a control that a screen reader says nothing about, so a blind user hears silence or a vague label while focus moves. Sighted keyboard users can also lose their place if the hidden control is off screen.
steps: Find the aria-hidden element in the scan result and note which link, button or field inside it can take focus.

If the content is meant to be hidden for everyone, such as a closed menu or an off-screen panel, hide it from all users with the hidden attribute or display: none, which also removes it from the tab order.
If the content should stay visible but unannounced, add the inert attribute to the container so nothing inside can be focused or clicked.
If the control should be usable, remove aria-hidden from it and from every ancestor.
When a panel opens or closes with script, update the hiding method at the same moment so the open state is never aria-hidden.
whyItMatters: Focus landing on something that is announced as nothing breaks the link between what a person hears and where they are. This is a WCAG 4.1.2 Level A requirement (Name, Role, Value), the level that accessibility regulations and procurement requirements commonly build on.
howToCheck: Press Tab repeatedly through the page and watch where focus goes. If it enters an area that should be closed or hidden, or a screen reader stays silent while focus moves, the problem is present.
